candidate.title: Reliability of machine-learning software effort estimation
candidate.workingTitle: Reliability of machine-learning software effort estimation
candidate.summary: Can software effort be estimated more reliably at task level using engineering context and actual active person-hours, while expressing uncertainty rather than producing an unsupported point estimate?
candidate.shortDescription: An alternative AI/software-engineering thesis direction focused on methodological reliability and task-level effort estimation, not another generic algorithm leaderboard.
candidate.technicalContribution: A task-level effort-estimation model/protocol that tests the incremental value of acceptance-criteria complexity/ambiguity, affected-codebase complexity, architecture/dependencies, technology stack/toolchain, and developer familiarity with the codebase/framework/language. Active person-hours is the preferred target; story points are secondary and team-calibrated only.

feasibility.rationale: This is a planning assessment. Public datasets exist in this literature, but the gap is not chosen.

candidate.dataRequirements: Candidate public data leads discussed include TAWOS, CHOET, AgES, and public software repositories; exact availability, schema, licensing, and feature coverage need verification. The proposed contextual features may require prospective task records. A prospective dataset should distinguish estimated effort, elapsed duration, and actual active person-hours.
candidate.evaluationDesign: Compare a historical/project-level baseline, acceptance-criteria-only features, task+codebase features, task+developer familiarity features, a full feature model, and a human estimate baseline where feasible. Use ablation to test each feature group, leakage-aware and temporal/cross-project validation where possible, and uncertainty evaluation. Assess actual active person-hours as target; do not treat story points as universal units.
majorRisks: The Scopus set has not yet been reconciled into a defensible single gap; familiar dataset/model comparisons are unlikely to be novel.
Public datasets may not contain the task-level contextual features proposed.
Linking tasks to actual active person-hours may be difficult and may require prospective data collection.
Story points are team-relative and not a universal measure of effort.
The feature set may become too broad for the MPhil timeframe.
openDecisions: Which methodological gap is supported by the Scopus evidence: task-level features, generalisation, uncertainty, or a tightly bounded combination?
Can task features be linked to actual active person-hours in public or prospective data?
Can the public datasets TAWOS, CHOET, or AgES support the intended feature/target combination?
Can developer familiarity be captured without privacy or proxy-variable problems?
What is the minimum viable prospective sample and validation plan?

nodes.title: Effort-estimation accuracy is hard to compare
nodes.summary: Machine-learning effort studies often cannot be lined up, because datasets, metrics, and splits differ.
nodes.detail: The project discussions considered AI in software development and software effort estimation. A generic comparison of algorithms on familiar datasets was rejected as insufficiently distinctive. A more concrete problem is that effort estimates may be unreliable when they ignore task-specific engineering context, fail to generalise across projects/teams, or provide point estimates without indicating uncertainty. The preferred target discussed was actual active person-hours, not story points as if they were universally comparable. The detailed feature proposal included acceptance-criteria complexity and ambiguity, affected-codebase complexity, architecture/dependencies, stack/toolchain, and developer familiarity with the codebase, framework, or language. The preferred target discussed was active person-hours. Story points were considered secondary because they are team-relative.

nodes.title: How can task-level engineering context improve the reliability and uncertainty of software effort estimates?
nodes.summary: How sensitive are selected effort models to the dataset, the project mix, leakage, and the validation protocol?
nodes.detail: The central direction is to estimate active person-hours for software tasks using features such as acceptance criteria, affected-codebase complexity, technology stack, and developer familiarity with that technology. The study must first determine whether the data can support these features and whether prior work already addresses them. Cross-project generalisation, temporal shift, uncertainty, and task-level features are candidate methodological angles, not all mandatory thesis components. Candidate baselines discussed were historical/project-level estimates, acceptance-criteria-only features, task+codebase features, task+developer-familiarity features, a full model, and a human estimate. The research should use ablation rather than a single leaderboard.

nodes.title: A methodological contribution, if one gap is chosen
nodes.summary: The literature base is large. The thesis needs one defensible hole in how estimation is evaluated.
nodes.detail: The IT contribution would be a measurable predictive method and evaluation protocol for software engineering work. The study should not become a project-management survey or a generic comparison of machine-learning algorithms.

nodes.title: One methodological focus
nodes.summary: One methodological focus
nodes.detail: One selected methodological focus, justified from the reconciled literature. Candidate foci are cross-project/temporal generalisation, calibrated uncertainty, and task-level engineering-context features. A possible controlled feature study can compare historical/project-level features, acceptance-criteria-only, task+codebase, task+developer familiarity, and full feature sets, with a human estimate baseline where feasible.

nodes.title: A repeatable protocol
nodes.summary: A repeatable protocol
nodes.detail: A repeatable estimation and evaluation protocol with a clear target definition, feature extraction, missing-data handling, train/test strategy, baselines, and reproducibility controls. The protocol should distinguish actual active person-hours from elapsed duration and story points, and should include leakage-aware, temporal, or cross-project validation where data permits.

nodes.title: Studies use different datasets and protocols

nodes.detail: The Scopus discussion identified studies including Ali (2022), Pospieszny et al. (2018), Sousa et al. (2023), Mahdi et al. (2021), Behdinian et al. (2022), Rahman et al. (2023), Raman et al. (2024), Rajput et al. (2025), and Chakravorty et al. (2025). The project had separate Scopus exports for effort-estimation literature. Their exact methods, datasets, and validation protocols still need reconciliation; the citation records are not all verified.

nodes.title: Reported accuracy may not travel across projects or datasets
nodes.summary: Reported accuracy may not travel across projects or datasets
nodes.detail: The potential issue is comparability and generalisation: reported performance may depend on dataset, project composition, target definition, and validation strategy. The Scopus studies must be reconciled before claiming that cross-project or temporal validation is missing. This branch remains one possible methodological focus.
risks: A generic algorithm bake-off on a familiar dataset is unlikely to be enough.

nodes.title: Point estimates dominate the notes
nodes.summary: Point estimates dominate the notes
nodes.detail: The literature notes identified task-level estimation work, including Sousa et al. (2023), but did not establish whether the reviewed models provide calibrated prediction intervals or other trustworthy uncertainty estimates. Full-text extraction is required.

nodes.title: A point estimate can hide tasks that should not be trusted
nodes.summary: A point estimate can hide tasks that should not be trusted
nodes.detail: A point estimate may conceal tasks for which the model is unreliable. The proposed contribution would be to estimate uncertainty and identify when an estimate should be treated cautiously or withheld. Whether this is novel relative to the reviewed papers is unconfirmed.

nodes.title: Uncertainty-aware estimates for task-level effort
nodes.summary: Uncertainty-aware estimates for task-level effort
nodes.detail: Investigate uncertainty-aware estimation for software-task effort, with active person-hours as the preferred target if it can be measured. Evaluate both point-estimate error and whether uncertainty meaningfully identifies high-error or out-of-distribution tasks. A human estimate baseline was also discussed, where feasible, so model performance is not interpreted without reference to actual estimation practice.

nodes.title: Can uncertainty estimates identify software tasks for which an effort prediction should not be trusted?
nodes.summary: Can uncertainty estimates identify tasks for which the model should not be trusted?
nodes.detail: Assess whether prediction intervals, calibrated uncertainty, or another justified uncertainty method can identify tasks with high estimation error or unfamiliar feature profiles.

nodes.title: Task-level features, including LLM-derived ones
nodes.summary: Task-level features, including LLM-derived ones
nodes.detail: Agile task estimates may need different inputs from classical project attributes.

nodes.title: Project-level attributes are the common feature set
nodes.summary: Project-level attributes are the common feature set
nodes.detail: The discussions moved beyond project-level attributes toward task-specific context: acceptance criteria, complexity of the affected codebase, technology stack, and the developer’s familiarity with that technology. These are proposed features, not features already confirmed in the public datasets. The feature proposal includes acceptance-criteria complexity/ambiguity; affected-codebase complexity and architecture/dependencies; technology stack/toolchain; and developer familiarity with the codebase, framework, or language. Public datasets may not contain these linked fields.

nodes.title: It is unknown whether task-level or LLM-derived features change the estimate
nodes.summary: It is unknown whether task-level or LLM-derived features change the estimate
nodes.detail: A possible contribution is to test whether task-level engineering context adds predictive value beyond conventional project-level attributes. LLM-derived task features were also discussed as a possible extension, but should not be included unless the Scopus review and data availability justify them. The proposed feature set must be operationalised and ablated.
validationRequirements: Check which reviewed datasets contain task-level records and actual effort values.
Define reproducible coding rules for acceptance criteria and codebase complexity.
Measure technology-stack and developer-familiarity features without leaking target information.
Use ablation to show which feature groups contribute.

nodes.title: Compare task-level features with conventional project attributes
nodes.summary: Compare task-level features with conventional project attributes
nodes.detail: Compare a baseline using conventional project attributes with a task-level model using acceptance-criteria characteristics, affected-codebase complexity, technology stack, and developer–technology familiarity. A prospective sample may be needed because public repositories often lack these linked features. LLM-derived features are an optional extension, not a required part of the thesis. Candidate public-data leads discussed include TAWOS, CHOET, and AgES, plus public software repositories. Their schema and suitability must be verified. If they do not contain actual active person-hours and task context, a prospective dataset may be required.
assumptions: Task-level records can be linked to actual active person-hours.
Acceptance criteria, codebase complexity, technology stack, and developer familiarity can be coded consistently.
risks: The public datasets may not contain the required contextual features.
Prospective collection may be needed and must fit the MPhil timeline.

nodes.title: Do task-level engineering-context features improve active person-hour estimates over conventional project-level attributes?
nodes.summary: Do task-level features improve estimates over conventional project-level attributes?
nodes.detail: Test incremental value using controlled baselines and ablation. The target should be actual active person-hours where reliable records exist; story points should not be treated as comparable across teams. The comparison should include ablation of acceptance criteria, codebase context, stack, and developer familiarity. The preferred target is active person-hours; story points should only be used as team-specific labels if their calibration is documented.
